title: A refused client certificate tells the peer nothing; the reason is debug-only
description:
Found 2026-11-22 on the live interop host while verifying the
[trusted_proxy] path (mimid-1wgh.46.20.1).

A peer whose client certificate mimid refuses receives:

    HTTP/2 403
    accept-signature: mimi=("@method" "@target-uri" "content-digest" "from");created;tag="mimi";alg="ed25519"
    content-type: application/problem+json
    {"status":403,"type":"tag:reviewcommit.com,2026:mimid:problem:provider-authentication"}

The actual reason -- for example "certificate refused: no dNSName for
the domain", or the "no credentials" case where no certificate arrived
at all -- is logged by mimid at DEBUG and never sent. Default log level
is INFO, so it is not even in the operator's journal.

Why this matters: the Accept-Signature header correctly steers a peer to
the RFC 9421 signature mechanism, which is right as a default. But it
means a PKIX or DANE misconfiguration is INDISTINGUISHABLE from "this
server wants signatures". A peer with a certificate that is one SAN away
from working would read the answer as "use signatures instead" and never
learn the certificate was nearly right. Both sides then see a 403 with
no way to converge, which is the worst shape for an interop day.

Two things to consider, separately:

1. mimid: give a distinguishable problem type, or a problem-detail
   field, when a certificate WAS presented and was refused, versus when
   none was presented. Take care not to turn it into an oracle: say
   enough for a cooperating peer to fix its configuration, not enough to
   help probe trust anchors. "A certificate was presented and rejected"
   plus a coarse category (name mismatch, path validation, expiry)
   looks like the right line. Note the mtls_binaries.rs tests already
   assert exact reasons are LOGGED, so the categories exist internally.

2. The draft (draft-atwood-mimi-provider-auth-00): consider saying a
   target provider SHOULD distinguish "no credential presented" from
   "credential presented and refused" in its response, since a peer
   cannot otherwise tell a policy decision from a misconfiguration.
   Posting needs Mark's OK, as every upstream post does.

Also worth deciding: whether these refusals should log at INFO rather
than DEBUG, so an operator running at the default level can see peer
authentication failures at all. Right now they cannot.
